# gRPC protocol reference

Rimsky talks to your service over gRPC. This reference lists every RPC rimsky's wire contract declares, the message each one carries, and the behavior rimsky expects on both sides of the call. Read the section for the protocol you implement, then prove your implementation with `rimsky conformance`.

The contract is ten `.proto` files declaring nine gRPC services and 36 RPCs, all in proto package `rimsky.v1`. A full method path therefore reads `/rimsky.v1.Executor/Execute`.

## Get the definitions

The npm package `@rimsky-ai/protocols` ships the ten `.proto` files, a `protoDir` constant, and a `protoPath(file)` helper.

The package ships **no generated stubs**. Its two exports are a directory path and a function that joins a filename onto it. Point `@grpc/proto-loader` or your own protobuf toolchain at `protoDir` and generate the clients yourself. A TypeScript author who expects to install the package and import a client gets the wire definitions and a path instead.

## The protocol files

| File | Service | RPCs | Who dials |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `executor.proto` | `Executor` | 1 | rimsky calls your service |
| `executor_observability.proto` | `ExecutorObservability` | 3 | rimsky calls your service |
| `claim_producer.proto` | `ClaimProducer` | 7 | rimsky calls your service |
| `claim_producer_observability.proto` | `ClaimProducerObservability` | 5 | rimsky calls your service |
| `data_processing.proto` | `DataProcessing` | 7 | rimsky calls your service |
| `lifecycle.proto` | `LifecycleSubscriber` | 7 | rimsky calls your service |
| `publisher.proto` | `Publisher` | 4 | rimsky calls your service |
| `validation.proto` | `Validation` | 1 | rimsky calls your service |
| `host_daemon.proto` | `HostDaemon` | 1 | your daemon calls rimsky |
| `events.proto` | none | 0 | payload shapes only |

## How rimsky reaches your service

Declare the service under one of the five service blocks in `rimsky.yml` — `claim_producers`, `executors`, `publishers`, `validators`, `data_processors` — keyed by the name templates use.

```yaml
claim_producers:
  files:
    endpoint: "grpc://files-producer:9100"
    write_semantics_allowed: ["sync"]
    protocols: ["claim_producer", "validation", "lifecycle_subscriber"]
    observability_endpoint: "grpc://files-producer:9100"
executors:
  http:
    endpoint: "grpc://http-node:9091"
    protocols: ["executor"]
```

**`endpoint`.** Write `grpc://host:port`, or a bare `host:port`. Rimsky strips the `grpc://` prefix and dials the rest. An `http://`, `https://`, `tcp://`, or `unix://` endpoint stops the process with `endpoint scheme must be grpc:// (got http://)`.

**`protocols`.** The list of protocols this service serves on that one endpoint. The six accepted tokens are `claim_producer`, `executor`, `publisher`, `validation`, `data_processing`, and `lifecycle_subscriber`; any other token stops the process with `unknown protocol`. One binary may register several protocol handlers on one gRPC server and list them all here. Each block's own protocol is mandatory in its entries' lists — a `claim_producers` entry must list `claim_producer`, an `executors` entry `executor`, and so on — and omitting the key altogether defaults to exactly that one token.

**`tls`.** Either `off` or `required`. Under `required` rimsky dials with TLS verified against its configured roots. The default is `off`, or `required` when the deployment sets `service_auth: mtls`.

**`service_auth: mtls`.** The deployment-wide mutual-TLS posture. Under it your service enrolls with the control API by api-key, receives a leaf certificate from the deployment CA, renews it automatically, and serves TLS requiring client certificates. Configure enrollment through `RIMSKY_SERVICE_AUTH`, `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_URL`, `RIMSKY_API_KEY`, and `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_CA`.

**`observability_endpoint`.** Where rimsky probes the observability sibling. Leave it unset and rimsky probes the primary `endpoint`.

**When rimsky calls each handshake.** Rimsky calls `ClaimProducer.Capabilities` on every `claim_producers` entry as a role process starts, with a 30-second timeout, and stops the process when the call fails or when the advertised `write_semantics_allowed` does not cover what the operator declared. It probes `ExecutorObservability.Capabilities` and `ClaimProducerObservability.Capabilities` at the same point, best-effort: an unreachable service is recorded as unreachable and startup continues. It calls `Publisher.Capabilities` later, when a template that names the publisher registers.

## Executor — `executor.proto`

An executor does the work of one node. Rimsky dispatches one node run to it and reads exactly one outcome.

### `Executor.Execute(ExecuteRequest) → Outcome`

Unary. There is no streaming form.

`ExecuteRequest` carries:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `node_id` | string | The node this dispatch runs. |
| `instance_id` | string | The instance the node belongs to. |
| `node_type` | string | The node's declared type. |
| `attributes` | `google.protobuf.Struct` | The node's resolved attributes, after substitution. |
| `attributes_schema` | `google.protobuf.Struct` | The merged effective JSON Schema for those attributes. |
| `claim_producers` | `map<string, ClaimProducerHandle>` | Acquired claims, keyed by claim alias — by producer name when the claim declares no alias. |
| `callback_url` | string | Base URL of the supervisor's callback listener. |
| `cancel_token` | string | Per-dispatch bearer credential for the two incremental callback routes. |
| `dispatch_id` | string | This dispatch's identifier. |
| `prior_dispatch_id` | optional string | The dispatch this one supersedes, when there is one. |
| `prior_dispatch_disposition` | optional `PriorDispatchDisposition` | Why it superseded that one. |
| `run_scope_id` | string | The execution context — root graph, sub-graph, or fan-out partition. |
| `scratch` | bytes | Your own opaque bytes from the superseded dispatch; empty on a fresh dispatch. |

`PriorDispatchDisposition` is `PRIOR_NONE`, `PRIOR_STALE_RECOVERY`, `PRIOR_RETRY_AFTER_ERROR`, or `PRIOR_RECALCULATE`.

`ClaimProducerHandle` carries `kind` (string), `handle` (`Struct` — the producer's address, payload, scope, and alias), and `candidate_handle` (bytes, set when the claim's producer implements the data-processing protocol).

Fields 4, 10, 11, and 13 are reserved (`userdata`, `resumed`, `run_attempt`, `resume_context`). They are gone from the contract. Do not send them.

### The `Outcome` oneof

Return exactly one of four variants.

**`Success`** — the run settled and the node is fresh. Carries `changed` (bool, drives the downstream cascade), `change_summary` (string), `attributes_delta` (`Struct`), `scratch` (bytes), and `tags` (repeated string).

**`Error`** — the run failed. Carries `error_class` (string, routed by the template's `error_types` policy), `payload` (`Struct`, opaque to rimsky), `scratch`, `attributes_delta`, and `tags`.

**`Park`** — the run pauses and resumes later. Carries `resume_at` (`google.protobuf.Timestamp`, **required**), `scratch`, and `tags`. Park carries no attributes delta; fields 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, and 8 are reserved.

**`AwaitAsyncCallback`** — the verdict comes later over HTTP. Carries `async_ack_id` (string, **required**) and `expected_completion_ms` (int64). Rimsky does not read `expected_completion_ms`; the node's own dispatch deadlines bound the wait.

Rimsky settles a malformed outcome as an error of class `executor_protocol_violation`: a `Park` without `resume_at` gives reason `park_missing_resume_at`, an `AwaitAsyncCallback` without `async_ack_id` gives `await_async_missing_ack_id`. An `Outcome` with no variant set settles as `executor_returned_unknown_outcome`, and a nil `Outcome` message settles as `executor_returned_nil_outcome`.

### Scratch

Scratch is your per-dispatch state and rimsky never reads it. Attach bytes to a settling outcome and rimsky persists them; the next dispatch that supersedes this one — in-place retry, stale recovery, cascade recalculate, or a park resume — hands them back in `ExecuteRequest.scratch`. A dispatch with no predecessor starts with empty scratch. There is no mid-dispatch scratch channel, and no resume-context field: park-and-resume state travels through scratch.

### Tags

Every settling outcome may carry tags, and subscribers filter on them. Declare the full set in `ExecutorObservability.Capabilities.declared_tags`. Rimsky rejects a template subscription that names a tag outside your advertisement, and settles a dispatch that emits one as `executor_protocol_violation` with reason `undeclared_tag`.

### Error classes

`error_class` is a free string, conventionally namespaced `<prefix>/<name>` — the bundled HTTP executor declares `http/network_error`, `http/timeout`, `http/expectation_mismatch`, and six more. Declare what you emit in `ExecutorObservability.Capabilities.declared_error_classes`; a declaration may end in `/*` to cover a family.

Eight classes are rimsky's own and you never emit them: `template_resolution_failed`, `template_validation_failed`, `executor_schema_unavailable`, `attributes_schema_failed`, `unresolved_executor`, `executor_sync_timeout`, `executor_protocol_violation`, and `abandoned`. Rimsky also synthesizes the `acquire/*` family when claim acquisition fails.

Declare each exact class you emit, even where a `/*` entry would cover it. Rimsky routes an error by looking the exact class string up in the node's `error_types` map, and no key in that map is ever a wildcard. A `/*` declaration therefore silences the registration warning while leaving the template author's policy unable to fire on a real failure.

### The async callback

After returning `AwaitAsyncCallback`, deliver the verdict by POSTing to `${callback_url}/v1/callback/{async_ack_id}` with an `AsyncCallbackBody` JSON body:

```json
{"success": {"changed": true, "change_summary": "wrote 4 rows", "tags": ["ok"]}}
```

Set exactly one of `success`, `error`, or `park`. Zero or two settings return HTTP 400. Field 1 is reserved (`events`) and must not be sent. `park.resume_at` is required and must be RFC 3339. The legacy `{"type": "complete"}` discriminator is gone and returns 400.

A 200 response carries `{"ack_status": ...}`, one of `accepted`, `rejected_run_terminal`, `rejected_run_stale`, `rejected_run_parked`, or `rejected_unknown`; a rejection other than `rejected_unknown` also names `current_node_run_id` when a successor run exists. An unknown ack id returns 404.

The `async_ack_id` is a correlation key, never a credential — rimsky authenticates the return leg by mTLS service identity under `service_auth: mtls`, and binds the callback to the principal it dispatched to. The registry survives supervisor restarts, so retry your POST with backoff rather than dropping an outcome after one failure.

Two further routes report progress during a long dispatch, and both require the dispatch's `cancel_token` as `Authorization: Bearer <cancel_token>`:

- `POST ${callback_url}/v1/runs/{run_id}/keepalive` — extends the quiet-period deadline and renews claim expiry. Returns 204.
- `POST ${callback_url}/v1/runs/{run_id}/attributes` — merges `{"attributes_delta": {...}}` into the run's attributes, and also counts as progress. Returns 409 when the run is neither running nor held.

Both return 401 without the token and 404 for an unknown run.

### The HTTP+JSON bridge

An executor may serve `POST /v1/Execute` over HTTP with a protojson `ExecuteRequest` body and a protojson `Outcome` response, and rimsky will dispatch over it when the service entry sets `transport: http`. Under `tls: required` the endpoint must be an `https://` URL.

This is the only protocol rimsky itself dispatches over HTTP+JSON. See "Where the shape is not symmetric" below.

## Executor observability — `executor_observability.proto`

Optional. Rimsky probes it at startup and caches the answer.

- **`Capabilities(ExecutorCapabilitiesRequest) → ObservabilityCapabilities`** — the handshake. Answer with `supports_trace_get`, `supports_trace_stream`, `retention_after_terminal_seconds`, `custom_ui`, `http_bridge_url`, `expected_attributes_schema` (bytes — the JSON Schema rimsky enforces at template registration and again at dispatch after substitution), `declared_tags`, `declared_error_classes`, and `validation_supported_roles`.
- **`GetTrace(GetTraceRequest) → Trace`** — one dispatch's trace by `dispatch_id`. `Trace` carries `evicted`, `complete`, and repeated `TraceEvent`.
- **`StreamTrace(StreamTraceRequest) → stream TraceEvent`** — the same trace as a server stream.

`TraceEvent` carries `event_id`, `parent_event_id`, `timestamp`, `severity`, `category`, `message`, and `attributes`. `Severity` is `SEVERITY_UNSPECIFIED`, `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN`, or `ERROR`. `CustomUI` carries `ui_url`, `embed_mode` (`EMBED_MODE_UNSPECIFIED`, `LINK`, `IFRAME`, `BOTH`), and `dispatch_url_template`.

Rimsky reads `validation_supported_roles` from this handshake to decide which validation roles an executor service will answer.

## Claim producer — `claim_producer.proto`

A claim producer owns a resource and tells rimsky what was acquired. Rimsky holds the lock ledger; you hold the substrate.

- **`Capabilities(CapabilitiesRequest) → CapabilitiesResponse`** — the startup handshake. Rimsky requires it and refuses to start without an answer. Answer with `write_semantics_allowed` (repeated `WriteSemantics`), `supports_split_scope`, `supports_scopes_conflict`, `protocols` (the mix-ins you serve), `validation_supported_roles`, and `declared_error_classes`.
- **`Open(OpenRequest) → OpenResponse`** — acquire. The request carries `claim_id`, `producer_name`, `selector`, `intent` (`r` or `rw`), `alias`, `template_id`, `instance_id`, `run_scope_id`, `lifetime` (`subgraph` or `durable`), and opaque `data` bytes. Answer with the `result` oneof: `Acquired{address, payload, claim_scope, realized_write_semantics}` — all three byte fields opaque to rimsky — or `Unavailable{error_class}`.
- **`Commit(CommitRequest) → CommitResponse`** — the claim succeeded. The request carries `claim_id`, `claim_scope`, `address`, `lease_token`. Answer with `version_id` and `producer_metadata`.
- **`Abandon(AbandonRequest) → AbandonResponse`** — the claim failed; drop the staging. Same request fields, empty response.
- **`Release(ReleaseRequest) → ReleaseResponse`** — the claim ended without a verdict. Same request fields, empty response.
- **`SplitScope(SplitScopeRequest) → SplitScopeResponse`** — partition a claim for fan-out. Gated on `supports_split_scope`. The request carries `claim_handle_id` and opaque `partition_request` bytes; answer with repeated `SubScopeDescriptor{claim_scope_data, partition_key, producer_metadata, address, payload, lease_token}`.
- **`ScopesConflict(ClaimScopesConflictRequest) → ScopesConflictResponse`** — does claim scope A overlap claim scope B? Gated on `supports_scopes_conflict`. Producers that do not advertise it get rimsky's default: byte equality.

`WriteSemantics` is `WRITE_SEMANTICS_UNKNOWN`, `WRITE_SEMANTICS_SYNC`, `WRITE_SEMANTICS_STAGED_ASYNC`, `WRITE_SEMANTICS_BLOCKING_ASYNC`, or `WRITE_SEMANTICS_READ_ONLY`.

### What rimsky enforces

- **The advertised envelope binds.** Rimsky rejects an `Open` whose `realized_write_semantics` falls outside `write_semantics_allowed`, and refuses startup when the operator's `write_semantics_allowed` in `rimsky.yml` is not a subset of what you advertise.
- **Byte-equal scope means equal semantics.** Two `Open` calls returning byte-equal `claim_scope` must return the same `realized_write_semantics`.
- **Terminal verbs must be idempotent in `claim_id`.** Rimsky delivers `Commit`, `Abandon`, and `Release` at-least-once from a durable per-producer outbox. A crash between delivery and bookkeeping redelivers. A recovering producer receives a scope's undelivered terminals in order before any new `Open` against that scope.
- **Do not keep lock state and do not serialize internally on lock-shaped predicates.** Rimsky owns concurrency; a producer that blocks a second `Open` on the first fails conformance check `Serialization9b`.
- **`Unavailable.error_class` becomes the node's error class verbatim**, falling back to `acquire/unavailable` when you leave it empty. Namespace it — the bundled filesystem producer answers `fs/root_unavailable` — and declare it in `declared_error_classes`.

### The HTTP+JSON bridge

A claim producer may serve the protocol over HTTP+JSON at `/v1/capabilities`, `/v1/open`, `/v1/commit`, `/v1/abandon`, `/v1/release`, `/v1/split_scope`, and `/v1/scopes_conflict`. `rimsky conformance claim-producer --transport http` runs the full suite against it. Rimsky itself dials claim producers over gRPC only: a `claim_producers` entry pointing at the bridge stops the stack.

## Claim producer observability — `claim_producer_observability.proto`

Optional, and reuses `Severity` and `CustomUI` from `executor_observability.proto`.

- **`Capabilities(GetClaimProducerCapabilitiesRequest) → ClaimProducerObservabilityCapabilities`** — answer with `supports_claim_get`, `supports_claim_stream`, `supports_list_claims`, `retention_after_terminal_seconds`, `custom_ui`, `admin_views`, `http_bridge_url`.
- **`GetClaim(GetClaimRequest) → ClaimDetail`** — one claim by `claim_id`, with `state`, `address`, `payload`, `scope`, `opened_at`, `closed_at`, and `history`.
- **`StreamClaim(StreamClaimRequest) → stream ClaimEvent`** — that claim's events as they happen.
- **`ListClaims(ListClaimsRequest) → ClaimList`** — a page of `ClaimSummary`, filtered by `state_filter` and paged by `cursor` and `limit`, answering `next_cursor`.
- **`GetAdminView(GetAdminViewRequest) → AdminView`** — run one view you declared in `admin_views` by `view_name` with `params`, answering a column `schema`, `data`, and a `render_hint`.

`ClaimState` is `CLAIM_STATE_UNSPECIFIED`, `OPEN`, `COMMITTED`, `ABANDONED`, `RELEASED`, or `UNKNOWN`. `AdminViewDecl` carries `name`, `title`, `description`, and `params`; each `AdminViewParam` carries `name`, `type`, `description`, `required`.

## Data processing — `data_processing.proto`

An optional mix-in on a claim producer, for the typed-data version lifecycle. Advertise `data_processing` in `protocols` — in `ClaimProducer.Capabilities` and in the service's `rimsky.yml` entry. The protocol carries control plane only: data moves substrate-direct through the address `Open` returned.

- **`Capabilities(google.protobuf.Empty) → DataProcessingCapabilities`** — `data_shapes`, `materializations`, `partition_kinds`, `aggregators`, all repeated strings rimsky does not interpret. Rimsky does not call this RPC; `rimsky conformance data-processing` does.
- **`BeginCandidate(BeginCandidateRequest) → BeginCandidateResponse`** — open a candidate version for one sub-claim. Carries `claim_handle_id`, `sub_scope_descriptor`, `idempotency_key`; answers opaque `candidate_handle` bytes. **Idempotent on the `(claim_handle_id, idempotency_key)` pair**: a retry returns the existing handle. Rimsky calls this in the same transaction that inserts the sub-claim row, and passes the handle to the leaf executor.
- **`CommitCandidate(CommitCandidateRequest) → CommitCandidateResponse`** — promote the candidate. Answers `candidate_metadata`. Rimsky calls it at the leaf run's success terminal.
- **`AbandonCandidate(AbandonCandidateRequest) → google.protobuf.Empty`** — drop it. Rimsky calls it on failure, strict cancellation, or descendant cancellation.
- **`ListVersions(ListVersionsRequest) → ListVersionsResponse`** — repeated `VersionMetadata{version_id, committed_at, producer_metadata}` for a claim handle.
- **`ListPartitions(ListPartitionsRequest) → ListPartitionsResponse`** — repeated `PartitionDescriptor{partition_key, partition_metadata}` for a `(claim_handle_id, version_id)` pair.
- **`GetVersionSchema(GetVersionSchemaRequest) → GetVersionSchemaResponse`** — opaque `schema` bytes for that version.

At parent-claim resolution the aggregation policy decides promote or abandon. On promote, rimsky fires `ClaimProducer.Commit` on the parent, and you aggregate the registered candidates per the claim's declared aggregator, promote atomically, and return the `version_id` — which rimsky records on the claim handle and in its lineage ledger.

## Lifecycle subscriber — `lifecycle.proto`

Seven control-plane callbacks. Every one answers the empty `LifecycleAck`.

- **`OnTemplateRegistered(OnTemplateRegisteredRequest)`** — `template_hash`, `spec` (the canonical, re-hashable template bytes).
- **`OnTemplateDeployed(OnTemplateDeployedRequest)`** — `template_hash`, `tags`.
- **`OnTemplateUndeployed(OnTemplateUndeployedRequest)`** — `template_hash`.
- **`OnTemplateDeregistered(OnTemplateDeregisteredRequest)`** — `template_hash`.
- **`OnInstanceCreated(OnInstanceCreatedRequest)`** — `instance_id`, `template_hash`, `instance_key`, `params`, `service_bindings`, `owner_api_key_id`, `target_routing_identity`.
- **`OnInstanceTerminated(OnInstanceTerminatedRequest)`** — `instance_id`, `template_hash`, `terminated_at_unix_ms`.
- **`OnRunScopeTerminal(OnRunScopeTerminalRequest)`** — `run_scope_id`, `terminal_reason`, `instance_id`.

**Opt in by protocol list.** Add `lifecycle_subscriber` to the `protocols` of a `claim_producers`, `executors`, or `publishers` entry, and rimsky dials the same endpoint for lifecycle. Entries under `validators` and `data_processors` are not consulted for lifecycle. A service that does not opt in is silently skipped.

**Delivery is at-least-once and runs after the transition commits.** The transaction that performs a transition stages the delivery as a row in one persisted outbox. The control API stages the template events, instance-created, instance-terminated, and the run-scope terminals of the scopes a termination closes. The scheduler stages the run-scope terminal of a settling frame. The supervisor stages the sub-graph and fan-out-partition terminals. Every runtime role drains the same outbox, and the role that staged a row wakes its own drain as soon as the staging commits, so a delivery does not wait on the drain interval. A per-scope advisory lock serialises the delivery and the row's deletion, so replicas converge on one delivery per service. A failed delivery keeps its row, records the attempt and the error on it, and retries on a widening interval; the interval is the retry path alone. A slow handler holds up that service's stream for that object, not the transition.

**Make your handlers idempotent.** A crash between your acknowledgement and the row's deletion redelivers the event, and a genuine re-transition — redeploy after undeploy, re-registration after deregistration — legitimately fires the callback again.

The protocol carries the control plane only. Node-run transitions such as a node parking never arrive here; read the event log for those.

**A bridge exists.** A subscriber may serve the seven callbacks over HTTP+JSON at `/v1/on_template_registered`, `/v1/on_template_deployed`, `/v1/on_template_undeployed`, `/v1/on_template_deregistered`, `/v1/on_instance_created`, `/v1/on_instance_terminated`, and `/v1/on_run_scope_terminal`. Rimsky dials lifecycle subscribers over gRPC only.

## Publisher — `publisher.proto`

A publisher pushes messages into rimsky. One service process serves many instances; each subscription provisions a per-instance broadcaster.

- **`Capabilities(google.protobuf.Empty) → PublisherCapabilities`** — the capability handshake, called when a template naming this publisher registers. Answer with `supported_kinds` (repeated `PublisherKindCapability{kind, config_schema}`), `protocols`, and `validation_supported_roles`. A template naming a kind you do not advertise is refused at registration.
- **`Subscribe(SubscribeRequest) → SubscribeResponse`** — provision a broadcaster. Carries `publisher_subscription_id`, `instance_id`, `kind`, `resolved_config` (bytes, your kind's own shape), and `message_type`. Field 5 is reserved (`target_node`): the surface carries no receiver, because rimsky routes by message type against node-subscription edges. Persist the `message_type` and stamp it on every envelope you send.
- **`Unsubscribe(UnsubscribeRequest) → UnsubscribeResponse`** — tear the broadcaster down, by `publisher_subscription_id`.
- **`ListSubscriptions(google.protobuf.Empty) → ListSubscriptionsResponse`** — repeated `PublisherSubscriptionDescriptor{publisher_subscription_id, instance_id, kind, resolved_config, message_type, started_at}`.

Make `Subscribe` and `Unsubscribe` idempotent: the conformance suite calls each twice.

**Sending a message is HTTP, not gRPC.** POST to the control API at `/v1/instances/{id}/messages` with an `Idempotency-Key` header and a body naming your `publisher_subscription_id` and the message `type`. Rimsky checks that the subscription is live and bound to that instance, then derives the sender name from the subscription row — the sender you declare in the request is ignored for trust. An unknown message type, or a subscription that is neither active nor mounting, is refused.

Rimsky coordinates no replicas for you. Single-replica is the supported posture.

## Validation — `validation.proto`

One RPC, advertised by any service alongside its primary protocol. Rimsky calls it at template registration only, never at runtime.

**`Validate(ValidateRequest) → ValidateResponse`.**

`ValidateRequest` carries a `role` discriminator and exactly one matching context:

| `role` | Context | Fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `executor` | `ExecutorContext` | `node_alias`, `attributes_schema` (the merged effective schema), `claim_aliases` |
| `claim_producer` | `ClaimProducerContext` | `producer_name`, repeated `ClaimBinding{node_alias, claim_alias, selector, intent, lifetime, data, partition_request}` |
| `publisher` | `PublisherContext` | `publisher_name`, `kind`, `resolved_config` |
| `lifecycle_subscriber` | `LifecycleSubscriberContext` | `subscriber_name`, `template_id` |

`ExecutorContext` field 2 is reserved (`userdata`).

`ValidateResponse` carries `valid`, `errors`, and `warnings`, each finding a `ValidationFinding{class, message, path}`. **Registration is decided by `errors`, not by `valid`** — a non-empty `errors` list rejects the template and warnings surface to the operator. The conformance suite does check `valid`, so set it consistently with your findings.

**Rimsky learns which roles you answer from different places per service class.** A claim producer's roles come from `ClaimProducer.Capabilities.validation_supported_roles`; an executor's from `ExecutorObservability.Capabilities.validation_supported_roles`; a publisher's from `Publisher.Capabilities.validation_supported_roles`. A standalone entry under `validators` has no capability call at all — its roles are its `protocols` list minus `validation`.

Rimsky consults executor and claim-producer validators per node, and publisher and lifecycle-subscriber validators per template — every registered subscriber advertising the lifecycle role is consulted template-wide, since a subscriber is never named by the template. An unreachable validator warns by default; the deployment can set `unreachable_validator_policy: strict` to reject instead.

## Host daemon — `host_daemon.proto`

The one protocol where your code dials rimsky. The host-daemon proxy serves it; the dev-machine daemon connects out.

**`HostDaemon.Connect(stream ClientFrame) → stream ServerFrame`** — one bidirectional stream carrying every interaction.

`ClientFrame` sends one of `Register`, `HostDaemonHeartbeat`, `SpawnAck`, `Reaped`, `DispatchFrame`, or `LocalHttpForward`. `ServerFrame` sends one of `RegisterAck`, `HostDaemonHeartbeatAck`, `Spawn`, `Reap`, `DispatchFrame`, or `LocalHttpResponse`.

- **`Register`** — `api_key` (the api-key plaintext, or the `anonymous` sentinel), `daemon_label`, `daemon_version`, `local_callback_base_url`, `routing_label`. The proxy verifies the key against the control API and routes by the key id it reports. **`RegisterAck`** answers `proxy_version`, `displaced_prior`, and the `routing_identity` the proxy adopted — persist it and re-present it on reconnect so existing instances keep reaching you.
- **`Spawn`** — `spawn_id`, `binding`, `cwd`, `run_scope_id`, `expected_protocols`, `ready_timeout_seconds`. `Binding` carries `path`, `args`, `env`, `cwd`, `ready_timeout_seconds`. The daemon picks a free local port, sets `RIMSKY_DAEMON_PORT` in the child's environment, and polls it until the child's gRPC server answers. **A spawned binary must read `RIMSKY_DAEMON_PORT` and bind there** — there is no port handshake back, and a binary that binds elsewhere fails the readiness poll.
- **`SpawnAck`** — `spawn_id`, `status` (`SPAWN_STATUS_UNSPECIFIED`, `SPAWN_STATUS_READY`, `SPAWN_STATUS_FAILED`), the child's `capabilities` map, and `error`.
- **`Reap`** / **`Reaped`** — `spawn_id` plus `sigterm_grace_seconds`, answered with `spawn_id`, `clean`, `error`. Closing the stream reaps every live child.
- **`DispatchFrame`** — `spawn_id`, `protocol`, `payload`, `stream_id`, `kind` (`DISPATCH_FRAME_KIND_DATA`, `_HALF_CLOSE`, `_CANCEL`), `claim_producer_verb` (`CLAIM_PRODUCER_VERB_OPEN`, `_COMMIT`, `_ABANDON`, `_RELEASE`), and `rpc_method`.
- **`LocalHttpForward`** / **`LocalHttpResponse`** — relay a child's local HTTP callback: `forward_id`, `method`, `url`, `body`, `headers`, `spawn_id`, answered with `forward_id`, `status`, `body`, `headers`.
- **`HostDaemonError`** — `class` and `message`, carried by `SpawnAck` and `Reaped`.

The daemon authenticates by api-key over TLS against the proxy's pinned deployment-CA root, not by mTLS enrollment. The daemon-to-child loopback runs its own always-on mutual TLS from a local CA the daemon generates itself, separate from the deployment CA.

## Event payloads — `events.proto`

`events.proto` declares no service. It is the shape registry for rimsky's own structured payloads: every event-log row and every cascade signal payload is declared here and built from the generated type.

It carries the `OperationalKind` enum, the `Event` message (`id`, `instance_id`, `node_id`, `occurred_at`, `kind`, a `payload` oneof, and `payload_raw`), and the per-kind payload messages — among them `StateTransitionPayload`, `ErrorPayload`, `WorkStartedPayload`, `WorkCompletedPayload`, `ClaimAcquiredPayload`, `LockAcquiredPayload`, `AttributesCommittedPayload`, `FanOutDispatchedPayload`, and the settling-signal payloads such as `TerminalSuccessSignalPayload` and `TransientRetrySignalPayload`.

`Event.kind` is a string, not the enum: each `OperationalKind` maps to a wire form such as `auth.access_attempted` or `state_transition`. Read payload values as JSON types — numbers arrive as doubles, timestamps as RFC 3339 strings, and 64-bit integer fields as JSON strings per the protobuf JSON mapping.

Fields whose shape belongs to someone else — an executor's error payload, a template author's blob — are declared `google.protobuf.Struct` or `bytes`, and rimsky passes them through uninspected.

## Prove your implementation

`rimsky conformance` runs a suite against a live endpoint. It offers seven subcommands: `executor`, `claim-producer`, `publisher`, `validation`, `data-processing`, `lifecycle-subscriber`, and `probe`. Exit 0 means every check passed, 1 means a check failed, 2 means the invocation was wrong.

```
rimsky conformance executor --endpoint grpc://localhost:9091 --check-observability
rimsky conformance claim-producer --endpoint grpc://localhost:9100
rimsky conformance claim-producer --endpoint http://localhost:9110 --transport http
```

- **`executor`** runs nine scenarios: `execute_happy_path`, `attributes_serialization`, `malformed_attributes`, `tags_round_trip`, `park_emission`, `scratch_park_round_trip`, `cancel`, `async_handoff`, and `async_callback_survives_restart`. `--callback-bind` and `--callback-host` place the suite's callback receiver where a containerized executor can reach it. `--allow-live` runs against a non-stub endpoint, skipping the scenarios that need a stub. `--check-observability` adds the `ExecutorObservability` probe, and `--retention-test-seconds` drives a dispatch and re-reads the trace to verify eviction.
- **`claim-producer`** checks the capabilities envelope, `Open` uniformity, non-serialization, split-scope shape, and the scopes-conflict predicate, and skips the checks your capabilities do not claim. `--transport http` runs the same suite against the HTTP bridge. `--check-observability` adds the `ClaimProducerObservability` probe, and requires gRPC.
- **`publisher`** checks `Capabilities`, `Subscribe`, `SubscribeIdempotent`, `Unsubscribe`, `UnsubscribeIdempotent`, and `ListSubscriptions`, and adds `MessagePush` when you pass `--control-api` and `--instance-id`.
- **`validation`** checks `RoleDispatch`, `UnknownRole`, `ExecutorHappy`, `ExecutorMissingContext`, `ExecutorMalformedAttributesSchema`, `ClaimProducerHappy`, `PublisherHappy`, and `LifecycleSubscriberHappy`.
- **`data-processing`** checks `Capabilities`, the candidate lifecycle, `BeginCandidateIdempotent`, `AbandonCandidateExcludedFromListVersions`, and `AbandonCandidateRejectsCommitAfterAbandon`.
- **`lifecycle-subscriber`** drives the seven callbacks.

The conformance kit ships in the `rimsky` binary and as the `rimsky-conformance` image.

## Where the shape is not symmetric

Four assumptions the protocol set invites, and what it actually does.

**Not every service has `Capabilities`.** Five of the nine services declare it — `ClaimProducer`, `ClaimProducerObservability`, `DataProcessing`, `ExecutorObservability`, and `Publisher`. Four do not: `Executor`, `Validation`, `LifecycleSubscriber`, and `HostDaemon`. A client that opens every connection with a `Capabilities` handshake gets `Unimplemented` — "unknown method Capabilities for service …" — against those four. An executor advertises through `ExecutorObservability.Capabilities` instead; a lifecycle subscriber and a host daemon advertise nothing.

**Only two protocols have an observability sibling.** The shipped set declares `ExecutorObservability` and `ClaimProducerObservability` and nothing else. There is no `PublisherObservability`, `LifecycleSubscriberObservability`, `ValidationObservability`, or `DataProcessingObservability`. An `observability_endpoint` on a publisher, validator, or data-processor entry parses and the stack starts healthy, but nothing reads it: the observability read routes exist for executors and claim producers only, and a publisher never appears in the system summary.

**The `transport` selector is executor-only.** Rimsky dispatches over HTTP+JSON to executors that set `transport: http`, and the conformance kit drives claim producers over their bridge with `--transport http`. Everything else is gRPC. `rimsky conformance` answers `--transport "http" not supported; use grpc` for `executor`, `validation`, `data-processing`, `lifecycle-subscriber`, and `publisher`. A claim-producer entry pointing at an HTTP bridge stops the stack; an `observability_endpoint` pointing at an executor's HTTP bridge fails the gRPC dial with `http2: frame too large`, after which the executor's attribute schema never becomes visible and template registration fails. If you plan to implement `Validation`, `DataProcessing`, `Publisher`, `LifecycleSubscriber`, or `HostDaemon` over HTTP+JSON, there is no path.

**The conformance kit does not cover the host-daemon protocol.** `rimsky conformance host-daemon` prints `unknown subcommand "host-daemon"` and exits 2, as do `hostdaemon`, `host_daemon`, and `daemon`. Nothing in the kit proves a `HostDaemon` implementation. The two observability protocols are covered, but not as subcommands — `--check-observability` on the executor and claim-producer suites runs them.
